title: Stochastic Matching Bandits with Rare Optimization Updates
claim: Matching proceeds in stages: unknown pairwise utilities, policy-based assignment, then stochastic acceptance of at most one assigned candidate per resource.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, bipartite graphs with sub-captions (a)-(c)
description: Three side-by-side bipartite-graph panels with the same layout: four orange circles (agents 1-4) in a rounded orange box on the left, and three green squares (arms 1-3) in a rounded green box on the right. Panel (a) draws green edges of varying thickness from every agent to every arm, showing unknown utilities, with a 'utility' legend. Panel (b) shows a single light-blue arrow from each agent to its assigned arm under a policy, with an 'assigned' legend. Panel (c) shows the same assignments, with blue arrows for accepted agents and red crossed-out arrows for rejected ones. Each arm accepts at most one agent. The legend marks accepted and rejected, and the sub-captions below explain each step. The eye goes first to the colored edges.
caption: Illustration of the stochastic matching process with 4 agents ($N = 4$) and 3 arms ($K = 3$).
abstract: We introduce a bandit framework for stochastic matching under the multinomial logit (MNL) choice model. In this setting, $N$ agents on one side are assigned to $K$ arms on the other side, where each arm stochastically selects an agent from its assigned pool according to unknown preferences and yields a corresponding reward over a horizon $T$. The objective is to minimize regret by maximizing the cumulative revenue from successful matches. A naive approach requires solving an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem at every round, resulting in a prohibitive computational cost. To address this challenge, we propose batched algorithms that strategically limit the number of times matching assignments are updated to $Î(\log\log T)$ over the entire horizon. By invoking expensive combinatorial optimization only on a vanishing fraction of rounds, our algorithms substantially reduce overall computational overhead while still achieving a regret bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$.
